evidence.note: The Internet Archive metadata for the alternate upload gives a release date of May 10, 1940. A 1940 US film is free only if its notice was missing or its copyright was not renewed. I could not retrieve the Stanford renewal database or read the 1967-1969 Catalog of Copyright Entries volumes in this session, and I did not search the Copyright Office public catalog. I can't cite a renewal-absence result. The Internet Archive's Public Domain Mark on the other upload is not a rights determination. Check the renewal window by hand.
This is a sound film. The recorded track normally shares the film's own copyright status, so the score is undetermined for the same reason as the print. I found no separate music-copyright record.

evidence.note: The Internet Archive metadata credits an original story by Mildred Cram and Adele Comandini. I did not research whether the story was published separately or when, so its term is unconfirmed.

The Internet Archive page for the alternate upload says a colorized version was produced by Legend Films and released by 20th Century Fox in 2004 as 'Beyond Christmas'. It also says the uploaded print was digitally remastered by the National Film Museum, Incorporated. A faithful black-and-white copy adds no new US copyright. The colorization, and any added material, can carry its own protection.

editorial:
Beyond Tomorrow is a 1940 fantasy directed by A. Edward Sutherland, with an original story credited to Mildred Cram and Adele Comandini. The ghosts of three elderly industrialists killed in an airplane crash return to reunite a young couple they brought together. The Internet Archive gives a release date of May 10, 1940 for one upload, which also carries the alternate title 'And So Goodbye'. Its Christmas themes are why people look for a free copy.

A 1940 film is free in the US only if its copyright notice was missing or its copyright was not renewed. I could not confirm either from a primary record, so every layer here except restorations is undetermined. The renewal catalogs for 1967 to 1969 are the place to check. The trap is the colorized edition: Legend Films colorized the film and 20th Century Fox released it in 2004 as 'Beyond Christmas'. That colorization is a separate layer and should not be assumed free, even if the black-and-white original turns out to be.
faq: Is Beyond Tomorrow (1940) free to use?

Not confirmed. It is a 1940 film, so it is free only if its notice was missing or its copyright was not renewed. I could not verify either from a primary record. Check the 1967-1969 renewal catalogs using the links in the dossier. The Internet Archive's public-domain label is not a rights determination.
Can I use the colorized version of Beyond Tomorrow?

Use a black-and-white print instead. The Internet Archive page says Legend Films produced a colorized version, released by 20th Century Fox in 2004 as 'Beyond Christmas'. The colorization can be separately protected even if the original film is free.
